Wanted: Dead

By: Harri Vithi | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Was it a shootout or did police go too far?

Unique Selling Point:
We use social media video to reveal how the police's specialized unit may have gone too far.

Summary:
Extortion incidents in the Eastern Cape have been catching on like wildfire, prompting the Eastern Cape SAPS to open an extortion hotline for locals to report these crimes.
Premier Mabuyane has called for military intervention in order to limit the disruptions to state infrastructure, schools and local businesses.
The National Police Commissioner called for its National Intervention Unit to investigate.

It’s against this backdrop that two accused extortionists have been killed by the police’s National Intervention Unit (NIU) within the past 6 months. Both reportedly, in shootouts. Given their reputation it's unsurprising it's said, they will not be missed by many.


Further information:
This story is focused on Nyalara’s killing because the videos posted by civilians on the road on February 20th, have called the police version of events into question. The below is the police’s version:-

Nyalara was killed while he had been travelling along the N2 near Ndabakazi, in Butterworth with his heavily armed bodyguards when operatives from the National Intervention Unit (NIU) tried to stop and search them. The two vehicles were suspected of carrying unlicensed firearms. However, the vehicles sped off, leading to a high-speed chase from Tsomo to the N2 near Mission A/A.
“During the chase, the NIU attempted to stop the Fortuners, but one vehicle collided with the NIU vehicles and opened fire. The police returned fire, resulting in the deaths of six individuals, including Nyalara,” a police report stated.
Responding to a question from News24 at the release of the quarterly crime statistics, national police commissioner General Fannie Masemola confirmed Nyalara's death, saying: "The answer is yes [he was killed]. The police were pushed off the road and tried to stop those cars, but the occupants opened fire, and officers returned fire."

Namely:-

Was Nyalara’s killing a hit on a controversial extortionist, executed by an elite police unit?
Seven people - including VIP Security were killed, was extreme force unnecessarily used by police in order to rid the province of a nuisance?
Are private security firms knowingly protecting suspected criminals, which could be viewed as aiding and abetting depending on the nature of their activities during the escort?

This story seeks to explore these questions by:-
Speaking to a tactical security specialist who will analyse the available social media footage in order to shed light on best practice versus what is witnessed in the videos
Analysing the police version against the video accounts
Highlighting the legal requirements of private security firms as relates to the vetting of principals (i.e their clients)

MNet Text Script: Wanted Dead

(Govan): On the 20th of February this year, a small stretch of the N2 between Ndabakazi and Butterworth in rural Eastern Cape made headlines.

(Govan) This story is about an alleged criminal mastermind killed in a shootout with police… …Accused of extortion, murder and rape… …and yet he always managed to evade justice.

(Govan): This man – Yanga Nyalara – and six others were travelling from Cofimvaba to Mount Frere when they were stopped by the police… here - and seven kilometers down the road here.

(Govan) Police say a gun battle ensued, leaving all seven men DEAD.

(Govan) BUT the evidence just doesn’t add up.

(Govan) We ask: Is there a dark force moving within the police ranks intent on street justice?

(Govan) Nyalara was a known gangster and a wanted man. He was tried for a 2021 mass killing spree, but acquitted and released from prison last November.
Govan) He knew there was a target on his back - so he hired protection.
(Clara Mbatha)(Subtitles) Michael Shabangu was my partner.
(Clara Mbatha) (Subtitles) We’d lived together for five years and were planning on getting married later this year.

(Govan) Four armed officers from KZN VIP Protection were assigned to escort Nyalara and two of his associates from Cape Town to the Eastern Cape.
(Govan) Michael Shabangu was the team leader.
(Clara Mbatha) (Subtitles) Michael was a quiet person but, when it comes to his work, he was very professional.
(Govan) Michael’s fiancée, Clara Mbatha says that during the trip, he grew uneasy.
(Clara Mbatha) (Subtitles) He asked if I could do some research for him on the side on this person.
(Clara Mbatha)(Subtitles) I went on TikTok and saw the type of person he was, and sent all of that information to Michael.
(Govan) But it was already too late.
(Clara Mbatha) (Subtitles) On that day, I kept calling but I couldn’t reach him…
(Govan) According to media statements, the elite National Intervention Unit, or NIU had information that two vehicles were travelling through the area with firearms. Police gave chase but the suspects refused to stop. When they opened fire, the police retaliated.
(Govan) All seven men were shot dead.
(Govan) But eyewitnesses give a very different account.
(Govan) Who is telling the truth?
(Govan) In the weeks since the shootout, we’ve gathered evidence, GPS tracker records, and witness accounts…
(Govan) All to investigate how four private security guards became suspects on the NIU’s radar - and ended up dead.
(Govan) Four verified cell phone videos reveal what really happened that day
(Govan) We’re following the route taken by the convoy. Nyalara and his two associates travelled in a white SUV, while the four security officers followed in a dark grey Toyota Fortuner.
(Govan) The first stop was Cofimvaba Police station: a routine check-in. Team leader Michael alerted local police to the convoy’s presence and produced firearm licences for inspection.
(Govan) But even as Nyalara posed playfully with these officers, the NIU was reportedly on the hunt for him.
(Govan) I’m sitting in the back seat to tell the story from the security officers’ perspective, to see if the police’s version matches the facts and right now I’m not so sure.
(Govan) KZN VIP Protection claims the four security guards were murdered. But police insist all seven men were suspects.
(Govan) We ran background checks on Bonga Mtshali, Bulelani Mbasa, Michael Shabangu and Simon Ndaba. None of them had a criminal record.
(Govan) From Cofimvaba, the convoy headed towards the N2.
(Govan) This intersection is where the road from Cofimvaba and the N2 meet. It's the place where the police stopped Nyalara and his bodyguards for the first time.
(Govan) Let’s call it scene one.In the police version: The NIU tries to stop the seven suspects. But they speed off.
(Govan) Instead witnesses say the police block off the suspects on both ends of the intersection and then…
.
(Govan) Two police officers advance and call Nyalara to come out of his car; he doesn't comply but two VIP Security officers come out instead with their hands up.

(Govan) The road is under heavy construction and speeding is near impossible. In other words, the police’s claim that the suspects sped off is questionable at best.
(Govan) International law enforcement expert, Lobo Das Neves, analysed the cellphone footage for us.
(Govan) Is there anything that immediately stands out here?

(Lobo Das Neves) What we see from this angle is two security guards apparently in the prone position and two more security guards standing up-right.

(Lobo Das Neves) The police aren’t really paying any special attention to these people.

(Govan) They’ve left them alone

(Govan) Is that abnormal?

(Lobo Das Neves) So the correct police training procedures would be that all suspects are put into a prone position, their hands handcuffed behind their backs…

(Govan) At this point our source says the police disarmed the private security but didn't arrest them.

(Govan) So, what do we have so far? Police stop the convoy, the guards surrender, they’re allegedly disarmed and everyone leaves the scene. But according to police… none of this happened.

(Govan) It's from here that the police say a high speed chase ensued but the GPS tracker from the Security vehicles shows that they were travelling at an average of 55km/h an hour

Govan) To scene 2 - The Kill Zone.
(Govan) Police say, the NIU attempted to stop the convoy, but one vehicle collided with the NIU cars and opened fire, which the police returned.
(Govan) But IF it’s true the suspects had been disarmed, how did they fire at the police?
(Govan) And according to witnesses - it was the NIU that tried to push Nyalara’s convoy off the road… and the police fired first.
(Lobo Das Neves) So we hear a sound which is most probably gunfire
(Govan) Can you see from here if the police look like they’re in a defensive position
(Lobo Das Neves) This is not how these police officers should be behaving, they should be taking cover. It looks like they’re quite relaxed.

(Govan) Men wearing jeans and tshirts some in tracksuits that's how witnesses describe some of the police officers that took part in the operation
(Lobo Das Neves) Apparently they’re the police, they have nothing identifiable as such but we are assuming.
(Govan) Witnesses say one guard tried to flee and was shot in the back. Then police turned on the other guards.
(Govan) Next, the officers fired shots into the ground.
(Lobo Das Neves) It looks like they’re firing either through the vehicle or past the vehicle into the area on the opposite side of the street.
(Govan) Why would they fire like that?
(Lobo Das Neves) So there’s no justifiable cause for police officers to start firing rounds in a public place…
(Govan) This looks like they’re staging a crime scene.
(Das Neves) I can just say the behavior of the police officers at that time gives rise to suspicion
(Govan) One thing seems clear: these officers are not under threat.
(Govan) After spraying the scene with bullets, they walk away - sparing no glance for the three security officers left dead or dying in the vehicle.
(Govan) Das Neves accompanies us to scene two. As bullets flew, Nyalara and his associates tried to escape off the road - but were killed as well.
(Govan) Are you able to still collect forensic evidence so long after the shootout?
(Lobo Das Neves) Yes it's possible when looking at the marks over here, these marks are consistent with bullet strikes
(Lobo Das Neves) The one on this side over here is consistent with a high powered rifle and this one possibly from a handgun
(Clara Mbatha)(Subtitles)The security guards were hit along the head and shoulder area and Michael was also shot in the back through his bullet proof vest. That means he was not fighting.
(Govan) But what do we know about the man believed to be the NIU’s intended target. And why would police go through so much trouble to kill him?
(Govan) Yanga Nyalara’s story as “Bara” begins in Khayelitsha, Cape Town — a tight-knit yet violent-stricken community. Bara was both feared and revered.

(Govan) We’re about to meet a source who’s familiar with the inner workings of the underworld in Khayelitsha, and we’re doing that to get a better sense of who Nyalara really was.

(Hidden identity) (Subtitles) His main hustle was extortion, drugs.

(Govan) It’s reported Nyalara was a qualified teacher - but by 2016 he was a wanted gangster.

(Hidden Identity)(Subtitles) He joined the gang, the 27s. That's when you started to hear the name “Bara”.

(Govan) You have to kill someone to get into the gang.

(Hidden Identity) (Subtitles) That’s how he made his mark. He killed a lot of people.

(Govan) And Nyalara’s reason for being in the Eastern Cape was just as suspicious.
(Hidden Identity)(Subtitles) He was there to expand his extortion business in the taxi industry.
(Hidden Identity)(Subtitles) He was conducting meetings left, right and centre because he actually named himself as the chairperson of that side.
(Govan)) On that day, on the side of the highway, did Nyalara’s past catch up with him?

(Govan) Do you think that he was taken out in a hit?

(Hidden Identity)(Subtitles) I know so. He was taken out.

(Hidden Identity) Subtitles) SAPS realised that a long time ago, that it’s difficult to arrest this one. So the only way was to take him out.

(Govan) According to our source, the hit was carefully planned in meetings with the community.

(Hidden Identity) (Subtitles) If you can’t arrest this guy, the best way: he must die.
(Hidden Identity) (Subtitles) There’s only one type of justice that he deserves;he must meet his maker.”
(Govan) We asked the Independent Police Investigative Directorate whether it’s looking into a possible police hit. It says due to ongoing investigations it’s unable to respond to our questions.

(Govan) As for Michael and his colleagues, they seem to have merely been collateral damage.
(Clara Mbatha)(Subtitles) Now that they’re all dead, there is no evidence and we want to know the reason they were killed.

(Govan) Men wearing jeans and tshirts some in tracksuits that's how witnesses describe some of the police officers that took part in the operation (Lobo Das Neves) Apparently they’re the police, they have nothing identifiable as such but we are assuming. (Govan) Witnesses say one guard tried to flee and was shot in the back. Then police turned on the other guards. (Govan) Next, the officers fired shots into the ground. (Lobo Das Neves) It looks like they’re firing either through the vehicle or past the vehicle into the area on the opposite side of the street. (Govan) Why would they fire like that? (Lobo Das Neves) So there’s no justifiable cause for police officers to start firing rounds in a public place… (Govan) This looks like they’re staging a crime scene. (Das Neves) I can just say the behavior of the police officers at that time gives rise to suspicion (Govan) One thing seems clear: these officers are not under threat. (Govan) After spraying the scene with bullets, they walk away - sparing no glance for the three security officers left dead or dying in the vehicle. (Govan) Das Neves accompanies us to scene two. As bullets flew, Nyalara and his associates tried to escape off the road - but were killed as well. (Govan) Are you able to still collect forensic evidence so long after the shootout? (Lobo Das Neves) Yes it's possible when looking at the marks over here, these marks are consistent with bullet strikes (Lobo Das Neves) The one on this side over here is consistent with a high powered rifle and this one possibly from a handgun (Clara Mbatha)(Subtitles)The security guards were hit along the head and shoulder area and Michael was also shot in the back through his bullet proof vest. That means he was not fighting. (Govan) But what do we know about the man believed to be the NIU’s intended target. And why would police go through so much trouble to kill him? (Govan) Yanga Nyalara’s story as “Bara” begins in Khayelitsha, Cape Town — a tight-knit yet violent-stricken community. Bara was both feared and revered. (Govan) We’re about to meet a source who’s familiar with the inner workings of the underworld in Khayelitsha, and we’re doing that to get a better sense of who Nyalara really was. (Hidden identity) (Subtitles) His main hustle was extortion, drugs. (Govan) It’s reported Nyalara was a qualified teacher - but by 2016 he was a wanted gangster. (Hidden Identity)(Subtitles) He joined the gang, the 27s. That's when you started to hear the name “Bara”. (Govan) You have to kill someone to get into the gang. (Hidden Identity) (Subtitles) That’s how he made his mark. He killed a lot of people. (Govan) And Nyalara’s reason for being in the Eastern Cape was just as suspicious. (Hidden Identity)(Subtitles) He was there to expand his extortion business in the taxi industry. (Hidden Identity)(Subtitles) He was conducting meetings left, right and centre because he actually named himself as the chairperson of that side. (Govan)) On that day, on the side of the highway, did Nyalara’s past catch up with him? (Govan) Do you think that he was taken out in a hit? (Hidden Identity)(Subtitles) I know so. He was taken out. (Hidden Identity) Subtitles) SAPS realised that a long time ago, that it’s difficult to arrest this one. So the only way was to take him out. (Govan) According to our source, the hit was carefully planned in meetings with the community. (Hidden Identity) (Subtitles) If you can’t arrest this guy, the best way: he must die. (Hidden Identity) (Subtitles) There’s only one type of justice that he deserves;he must meet his maker.” (Govan) We asked the Independent Police Investigative Directorate whether it’s looking into a possible police hit. It says due to ongoing investigations it’s unable to respond to our questions. (Govan) As for Michael and his colleagues, they seem to have merely been collateral damage. (Clara Mbatha)(Subtitles) Now that they’re all dead, there is no evidence and we want to know the reason they were killed.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Was it a shootout or did police go too far?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We use social media video to reveal how the police's specialized unit may have gone too far.
metadata.Summary: Extortion incidents in the Eastern Cape have been catching on like wildfire, prompting the Eastern Cape SAPS to open an extortion hotline for locals to report these crimes. Premier Mabuyane has called for military intervention in order to limit the disruptions to state infrastructure, schools and local businesses. The National Police Commissioner called for its National Intervention Unit to investigate. It’s against this backdrop that two accused extortionists have been killed by the police’s National Intervention Unit (NIU) within the past 6 months. Both reportedly, in shootouts. Given their reputation it's unsurprising it's said, they will not be missed by many.
metadata.Further information: This story is focused on Nyalara’s killing because the videos posted by civilians on the road on February 20th, have called the police version of events into question. The below is the police’s version:- Nyalara was killed while he had been travelling along the N2 near Ndabakazi, in Butterworth with his heavily armed bodyguards when operatives from the National Intervention Unit (NIU) tried to stop and search them. The two vehicles were suspected of carrying unlicensed firearms. However, the vehicles sped off, leading to a high-speed chase from Tsomo to the N2 near Mission A/A. “During the chase, the NIU attempted to stop the Fortuners, but one vehicle collided with the NIU vehicles and opened fire. The police returned fire, resulting in the deaths of six individuals, including Nyalara,” a police report stated. Responding to a question from News24 at the release of the quarterly crime statistics, national police commissioner General Fannie Masemola confirmed Nyalara's death, saying: "The answer is yes [he was killed]. The police were pushed off the road and tried to stop those cars, but the occupants opened fire, and officers returned fire." Namely:- Was Nyalara’s killing a hit on a controversial extortionist, executed by an elite police unit? Seven people - including VIP Security were killed, was extreme force unnecessarily used by police in order to rid the province of a nuisance? Are private security firms knowingly protecting suspected criminals, which could be viewed as aiding and abetting depending on the nature of their activities during the escort? This story seeks to explore these questions by:- Speaking to a tactical security specialist who will analyse the available social media footage in order to shed light on best practice versus what is witnessed in the videos Analysing the police version against the video accounts Highlighting the legal requirements of private security firms as relates to the vetting of principals (i.e their clients)
